domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: Point-of-care ultrasound is described as a valuable alternative to chest X-ray for diagnosing pleural effusion. What other two diagnoses can POCUS simultaneously assess?
answer: POCUS can simultaneously identify pneumothorax and lobar consolidation in addition to pleural effusion, making it highly efficient in undifferentiated dyspneic patients.
rationale: Pleural effusion appears as an echo-free space above the diaphragm; lung consolidation appears hyperechoic; pneumothorax is identified by absence of lung sliding and presence of lung point.

domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: Approximately how many new cases of malignant pleural effusion are reported annually in the US and Europe combined, and what proportion of cancer patients develop MPE?
answer: Approximately 500,000 new MPE cases annually in the US and Europe combined; MPE affects up to 20% of cancer patients and can be linked to any cancer type.
rationale: MPE is one of the most common oncologic complications; the large volume of patients underscores the importance of palliative drainage strategies and symptom management in cancer care.

domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: Whispered pectoriloquy and egophony are found in what anatomical relationship to a pleural effusion on auscultation?
answer: Both whispered pectoriloquy and egophony may be appreciated at the UPPER BORDER of the pleural effusion, where compressed lung transmits sounds distinctively.
rationale: Fluid below attenuates sounds (dullness to percussion, reduced breath sounds); at the fluid-compressed lung interface above, sound transmission changes produce egophony (E-to-A change) and whispered pectoriloquy.

domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: Contrast-enhanced CT findings raising suspicion for malignant pleural effusion include what imaging features?
answer: Massive effusion, loculation, loss of volume of the ipsilateral lung (trapped lung), nodular pleural thickening, mediastinal pleural thickening, and circumferential pleural thickening suggest malignant etiology.
rationale: Malignant pleural deposits cause nodular/irregular thickening and may fix the lung (trapped lung); these CT features distinguish MPE from benign transudative effusions and guide biopsy site selection.
confusable_with: Mesothelioma vs pleural metastasis (CT cannot reliably distinguish)

domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: Thoracoscopic biopsy with immunohistochemistry significantly improves detection of malignant pleural effusion. What are the remaining limitations of cytological analysis?
answer: Low yield, difficulty distinguishing cell types without immunohistochemistry, and inability to distinguish malignant pleural mesothelioma from pleural metastasis on cytology alone are key limitations.
rationale: Mesothelial cells and adenocarcinoma cells can appear similar on cytology; immunohistochemistry panels (calretinin, WT-1 for mesothelioma; TTF-1, CEA for carcinoma) resolve this, making thoracoscopic biopsy the gold standard for difficult cases.

domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: In a patient with cardiac tamponade confirmed by POCUS, what is the definition that distinguishes it from simple pericardial effusion?
answer: Cardiac tamponade is defined as hemodynamic insufficiency caused by impaired cardiac filling due to elevated pericardial pressure from effusion, leading to equalization of intracardiac diastolic pressures.
rationale: Not all pericardial effusions cause tamponade; hemodynamic significance requires that pericardial pressure rises enough to impair diastolic filling, detectable as right chamber collapse and IVC plethora on POCUS.

domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: Fibrous septations and adhesions within a pleural effusion are differentiated by thoracoscopy. How do fibrinous adhesions differ from dense organized adhesions in terms of management?
answer: Fibrinous adhesions can be divided easily during thoracoscopy; dense organized adhesions cannot be easily broken down and may cause failure of an effusion to drain effectively, limiting thoracoscopic management.
rationale: Early thoracoscopic drainage addresses fibrinous loculations; established fibrous organization requires surgical decortication; this progression underscores the importance of early pleural drainage in parapneumonic effusions.

domain: General internal medicine, preventive care & geriatrics (admission & cross-cover problems, perioperative medicine, screening & vaccination, polypharmacy & deprescribing, frailty, delirium prevention, goals of care)
stem: Hospital-acquired pneumonia (HAP) is defined by onset at what point after admission, and how does VAP differ?
answer: HAP is pneumonia developing 48 or more hours after hospital admission in a non-intubated patient; VAP (ventilator-associated pneumonia) develops 48-72 hours after intubation and mechanical ventilation.
rationale: The 48-hour threshold distinguishes community-acquired from hospital-acquired pathogens; VAP represents a subset of HAP with the highest mortality due to selection pressure for multi-drug resistant organisms.

domain: General internal medicine, preventive care & geriatrics (admission & cross-cover problems, perioperative medicine, screening & vaccination, polypharmacy & deprescribing, frailty, delirium prevention, goals of care)
stem: Empiric treatment for VAP should cover which organisms based on institutional guidelines?
answer: Empiric VAP treatment must cover Pseudomonas aeruginosa, MRSA, and other multi-drug resistant gram-negative organisms; de-escalation is guided by culture results.
rationale: ICU patients on ventilators are colonized with hospital-acquired pathogens including resistant gram-negatives and MRSA; the high mortality of VAP mandates broad empirical coverage pending susceptibility data.

domain: General internal medicine, preventive care & geriatrics (admission & cross-cover problems, perioperative medicine, screening & vaccination, polypharmacy & deprescribing, frailty, delirium prevention, goals of care)
stem: Advanced age correlates strongly with aspiration pneumonia. What physiologic change in older adults drives this?
answer: Many older adults experience silent microaspiration of bacteria-rich oropharyngeal fluids; decreased cough reflex, impaired swallowing, and reduced immune surveillance make aspiration pneumonia common in the elderly.
rationale: Aging reduces gag reflex sensitivity, promotes pharyngeal dysmotility, and impairs mucociliary clearance; the resulting silent aspiration deposits oral flora (often anaerobes and gram-negatives) into lower airways.

source.book: StatPearls: StatPearls   Aspiration Pneumonia and Pneumonitis

confusable_with: Aspiration pneumonitis (chemical injury from acid, not bacterial)

domain: General internal medicine, preventive care & geriatrics (admission & cross-cover problems, perioperative medicine, screening & vaccination, polypharmacy & deprescribing, frailty, delirium prevention, goals of care)
stem: Aspiration pneumonia manifests across what clinical spectrum depending on aspirate content?
answer: Aspiration pneumonia manifests from aspiration of bacteria-rich oropharyngeal secretions (infectious aspiration pneumonia) to aspiration of gastric acid (chemical aspiration pneumonitis); particulate matter causes obstructive aspiration.
rationale: The clinical syndrome depends on whether the aspirate is primarily bacterial (oropharyngeal), acidic (gastric, pH<2.5), or particulate; each mechanism requires distinct management.

source.book: StatPearls: StatPearls   Aspiration Pneumonia and Pneumonitis

domain: General internal medicine, preventive care & geriatrics (admission & cross-cover problems, perioperative medicine, screening & vaccination, polypharmacy & deprescribing, frailty, delirium prevention, goals of care)
stem: Staphylococcal pneumonia presents as what clinical syndrome, and what radiographic appearance is characteristic?
answer: Staphylococcal pneumonia presents with broad, nonspecific pulmonary symptoms; community-acquired Staphylococcal pneumonia may cause pneumatoceles, empyema, and rapid cavitation; the differential is broad due to nonspecific presentation.
rationale: S. aureus produces toxins and proteases that cause extensive tissue destruction; pneumatocele formation from check-valve bronchiolar obstruction and necrotizing pneumonia are characteristic features not seen with typical community organisms.

domain: General internal medicine, preventive care & geriatrics (admission & cross-cover problems, perioperative medicine, screening & vaccination, polypharmacy & deprescribing, frailty, delirium prevention, goals of care)
stem: Gram-negative organisms account for most cases of infection-related SIRS. At what point does this protective response become harmful?
answer: A marked or prolonged SIRS response, as in severe pneumonia-associated sepsis, causes widespread organ dysfunction (ARDS, AKI, distributive shock) rather than remaining salutatory.
rationale: Moderate SIRS enhances immune defense; overwhelming activation of complement, coagulation, and cytokine cascades from gram-negative LPS causes endothelial damage, diffuse capillary leak, and multi-organ failure.

domain: General internal medicine, preventive care & geriatrics (admission & cross-cover problems, perioperative medicine, screening & vaccination, polypharmacy & deprescribing, frailty, delirium prevention, goals of care)
stem: Late admission to the ICU (rather than early) in patients with CAP is associated with what outcome?
answer: Late ICU admission in CAP patients is associated with higher mortality; early recognition of severity and timely ICU escalation improves survival.
rationale: CAP patients requiring ICU care who are managed in lower-acuity settings until clinical deterioration have delayed resuscitation, delayed broad-spectrum antibiotics, and delayed organ support, worsening outcomes.

source.book: Society Guideline: Guideline   IDSA ATS 2019 CAP Executive Summary

enabling_conditions: CAP: community exposure, advanced age, smoking, immunocompromise, asplenia; HAP/VAP: intubation >48h, ICU admission, prior antibiotics; Aspiration: dysphagia, altered consciousness, poor dentition, GERD
pathophysiology: Pathogen overcomes mucociliary clearance and alveolar macrophage defenses; alveolar consolidation from fibrinous exudate impairs gas exchange; gram-negative LPS triggers systemic inflammatory response
time_course: CAP: community onset, rapid progression in elderly/immunocompromised; HAP: 48h+ post-admission; aspiration: hours to days after aspiration event
key_features: Fever, productive cough, pleuritic chest pain, lobar consolidation on CXR; CURB-65 or PSI for severity; HAP/VAP: new infiltrate + fever + leukocytosis + purulent secretions after 48h admission
consequence_if_missed: Septic shock, ARDS, empyema, respiratory failure requiring intubation, death (mortality 5-15% CAP, 30-40% VAP)

domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: On pulmonary ultrasound, what is the most specific finding for pneumothorax?
answer: The lung point is the most specific finding for pneumothorax; it represents the boundary between aerated lung and pleural air, visible as alternating lung sliding and absent lung sliding at the pneumothorax margin.
rationale: The lung point has nearly 100% specificity for pneumothorax; its location indicates the size of the pneumothorax—a more posterior lung point indicates a larger pneumothorax.
confusable_with: Absent lung sliding alone (seen in mainstem intubation, apnea)

domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: When performing a lung ultrasound for pneumothorax in a supine patient, where should the probe be placed and why?
answer: The probe should be placed in the midaxillary line with indicator toward the patient's head; in a supine patient, air rises anteriorly, but positioning in the midaxillary or anterior chest identifies the highest point where pneumothorax collects.
rationale: Air rises to the non-dependent (anterior) pleural space in the supine patient; placing the probe anteriorly or moving posteriorly if no anterior sliding is found identifies the pneumothorax margins.

domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: Nitrous oxide expands closed gas spaces. What is the clinical implication for a patient with suspected or known pneumothorax undergoing general anesthesia?
answer: Nitrous oxide (blood:gas partition 0.47) has low solubility and expands nitrogen-containing closed spaces; it is absolutely contraindicated in pneumothorax because it rapidly enlarges the pneumothorax, potentially causing tension pneumothorax.
rationale: N2O diffuses into the gas-filled pleural space faster than nitrogen diffuses out; the resulting volume expansion of a pneumothorax can convert it to tension, causing cardiovascular collapse.

domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: Capnography shows a decreased EtCO2 with an increased A-a gradient between EtCO2 and PaCO2 in what two emergency conditions?
answer: Pulmonary embolism and significant pneumothorax both reduce perfusion of ventilated alveoli (increased dead space), decreasing EtCO2 while PaCO2 rises, widening the EtCO2-PaCO2 gradient.
rationale: EtCO2 reflects alveolar CO2 from perfused lung; when pulmonary blood flow is acutely reduced (PE) or lung is collapsed (pneumothorax), EtCO2 falls while arterial PCO2 rises, creating a diagnostic widening of the gradient.

domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: Tension pneumothorax and cardiac tamponade both cause obstructive shock. What physical examination and POCUS findings differentiate them?
answer: Tension pneumothorax: tracheal deviation, absent breath sounds unilaterally, absent lung sliding on POCUS; tamponade: muffled heart sounds, normal breath sounds, pericardial effusion with RV collapse on POCUS.
rationale: Both cause JVD and hypotension from obstructed cardiac filling; differentiating by physical exam (breath sounds) and POCUS (lung sliding vs pericardial effusion) enables rapid targeted treatment (needle decompression vs pericardiocentesis).

domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: In the setting of intraoperative hypotension, what cardiovascular formula defines mean arterial pressure?
answer: MAP - CVP = CO x SVR; equivalently MAP = CO x SVR + CVP; sudden hypotension with tachycardia, falling SpO2, and rising airway pressures suggests tension pneumothorax.
rationale: Understanding the determinants of BP allows systematic diagnosis of intraoperative hypotension; the constellation of rising airway pressure, reduced lung compliance, hypotension, and absent unilateral breath sounds distinguishes tension pneumothorax from other causes.

domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: Pulmonary ultrasound is superior to supine chest X-ray for detecting pneumothorax. Why?
answer: In a supine patient, air rises to the anterior pleural space which is not well seen on AP chest X-ray; POCUS identifies absent lung sliding and lung point anteriorly with high sensitivity and specificity.
rationale: Supine CXR misses up to 30% of pneumothoraces because the anterior pleural air is not seen on frontal projection; ultrasound directly images the anterior pleural surface at the bedside without radiation.

domain: Internal medicine: gastroenterology & hepatology (upper & lower GI bleed, acute liver failure, cirrhosis & its complications, pancreatitis, IBD, bowel obstruction, hepatic encephalopathy)
stem: What is the direct mechanism by which cirrhosis causes portal hypertension?
answer: Distortion of the liver's normal cellular and vascular architecture from fibrosis obstructs portal venous flow, directly raising portal pressure and leading to varices.
rationale: Sinusoidal fibrosis and regenerative nodule formation increase intrahepatic vascular resistance; portal pressure rises above the normal threshold of 5 mmHg, driving collateral vessel formation at portosystemic sites.

domain: Internal medicine: gastroenterology & hepatology (upper & lower GI bleed, acute liver failure, cirrhosis & its complications, pancreatitis, IBD, bowel obstruction, hepatic encephalopathy)
stem: What four major portosystemic collateral sites develop in portal hypertension?
answer: Esophageal/gastric varices (GE junction), rectal varices/hemorrhoids, periumbilical (caput medusae), and retroperitoneal collaterals; esophageal varices are the most clinically dangerous.
rationale: Portal pressure drives reversal of blood flow through pre-existing anastomoses between portal and systemic veins; esophageal varices rupture most commonly because their thin walls are exposed to the high portal-to-systemic gradient.

domain: Internal medicine: gastroenterology & hepatology (upper & lower GI bleed, acute liver failure, cirrhosis & its complications, pancreatitis, IBD, bowel obstruction, hepatic encephalopathy)
stem: Cirrhosis causes a hyperdynamic cardiovascular state. What are the hemodynamic features?
answer: High cardiac output, low systemic vascular resistance, systemic arteriovenous shunts, and cirrhotic cardiomyopathy; pulmonary hypertension and increased intrapulmonary shunting (hepatopulmonary syndrome) also develop.
rationale: Vasodilatory mediators (NO, prostacyclin) accumulate because the liver cannot degrade them; the resulting splanchnic vasodilation activates the RAAS and sympathetic system, creating a high-output, low-resistance state.

domain: Internal medicine: gastroenterology & hepatology (upper & lower GI bleed, acute liver failure, cirrhosis & its complications, pancreatitis, IBD, bowel obstruction, hepatic encephalopathy)
stem: Surgical procedures in cirrhotic patients carry excessive bleeding risk through what mechanisms?
answer: Venous engorgement from portal hypertension, varices, lysis of adhesions from previous surgery, and coagulopathy all contribute; evacuation of ascites and prolonged surgery cause large fluid shifts.
rationale: All four bleeding mechanisms operate simultaneously in cirrhosis; the coagulopathy (thrombocytopenia, low clotting factors), varices, and portal hypertension make surgical hemostasis far more challenging than in non-cirrhotic patients.

domain: Internal medicine: gastroenterology & hepatology (upper & lower GI bleed, acute liver failure, cirrhosis & its complications, pancreatitis, IBD, bowel obstruction, hepatic encephalopathy)
stem: Patients with acute hepatitis should have elective surgery postponed until when?
answer: Elective surgery should be postponed until the acute hepatitis has resolved, as indicated by normalization of liver function tests; the perioperative mortality risk is prohibitively high during active hepatitis.
rationale: Acute hepatocellular inflammation impairs all hepatic synthetic and metabolic functions; anesthesia and surgery further reduce hepatic blood flow and oxygen delivery, risking acute hepatic failure.
confusable_with: Chronic stable cirrhosis (higher but accepted perioperative risk)

domain: Internal medicine: gastroenterology & hepatology (upper & lower GI bleed, acute liver failure, cirrhosis & its complications, pancreatitis, IBD, bowel obstruction, hepatic encephalopathy)
stem: Hepatorenal syndrome can be treated with what vasoconstrictor combination, and when does ATN develop if untreated?
answer: Hepatorenal syndrome is treated with vasoconstrictors (vasopressin analogue terlipressin, or vasopressin plus midodrine plus norepinephrine) and IV albumin; prolonged kidney impairment eventually results in ATN if not reversed.
rationale: HRS results from splanchnic vasodilation reducing effective renal perfusion; vasoconstrictors redistribute blood to the kidney; terlipressin is the most evidence-based agent, reversing HRS in 40-50% of cases.

domain: Internal medicine: gastroenterology & hepatology (upper & lower GI bleed, acute liver failure, cirrhosis & its complications, pancreatitis, IBD, bowel obstruction, hepatic encephalopathy)
stem: Cirrhosis may result in all of the following except one. Which systemic complication is NOT a direct consequence of portal hypertension?
answer: Bleeding varices, ascites, HRS, hepatic encephalopathy, and coagulopathy are all direct complications; the hyperdynamic circulation with high CO and low SVR can cause cirrhotic cardiomyopathy—however, the answer depends on which option is presented. The key teaching is that cirrhosis causes widespread organ dysfunction through portal hypertension AND toxin accumulation (not cleared by liver).
rationale: Cirrhosis causes both portal hypertensive complications (varices, ascites, SBP) and hepatocellular failure complications (coagulopathy, HE, HRS); distinguishing these mechanisms guides therapy.

domain: Internal medicine: cardiology (ACS, stable & unstable angina, heart failure, brady/tachyarrhythmias, valvular disease, hypertension & emergencies, lipids, syncope)
stem: In the ACC/AHA stepwise algorithm for preoperative cardiac evaluation, what is Step 1 and what determines the decision at Step 2?
answer: Step 1: determine if surgery is emergent (proceed, optimize post-operatively). Step 2: assess for active cardiac conditions (unstable angina, decompensated HF, severe valvular disease, significant arrhythmias)—if present, delay and treat before elective surgery.
rationale: Active cardiac conditions represent high acute risk that must be stabilized before elective surgery; emergent cases cannot wait and require intraoperative management of known cardiac risk.

domain: Internal medicine: cardiology (ACS, stable & unstable angina, heart failure, brady/tachyarrhythmias, valvular disease, hypertension & emergencies, lipids, syncope)
stem: Preventing postoperative pulmonary complications is also an important goal of preoperative cardiovascular assessment. What two patient conditions drive both cardiac and pulmonary perioperative risk simultaneously?
answer: OSA and COPD drive both cardiac and pulmonary perioperative risk simultaneously; OSA causes pulmonary hypertension and right heart failure; COPD causes pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale.
rationale: OSA generates recurrent hypoxemia and elevated pulmonary artery pressure; COPD causes chronic hypoxic vasoconstriction; both impair cardiac reserve and respiratory reserve together.

domain: Internal medicine: cardiology (ACS, stable & unstable angina, heart failure, brady/tachyarrhythmias, valvular disease, hypertension & emergencies, lipids, syncope)
stem: What intraoperative finding on ECG monitoring most dramatically increases perioperative cardiac event risk, and by how much?
answer: ST-segment elevation or depression increases cardiac event risk 10-fold and the risk of death 2-fold; these are intraoperative signs of myocardial ischemia.
rationale: Intraoperative ischemia may progress to myocardial infarction if not identified and treated; the 10-fold increase in events emphasizes the need for continuous ECG monitoring and prompt intervention when ST changes occur.

domain: Internal medicine: cardiology (ACS, stable & unstable angina, heart failure, brady/tachyarrhythmias, valvular disease, hypertension & emergencies, lipids, syncope)
stem: OSA-related critical events were analyzed in a registry created by SASM. What type of events were characterized?
answer: Life-threatening perioperative events in OSA patients were characterized to generate evidence-based guidance for prevention and management of OSA-related complications in anesthesia.
rationale: The registry approach enables identification of specific OSA-related risk scenarios (postoperative respiratory failure, difficult airway, reintubation) and the effectiveness of preventive strategies (CPAP, monitoring, opioid reduction).

domain: Internal medicine: cardiology (ACS, stable & unstable angina, heart failure, brady/tachyarrhythmias, valvular disease, hypertension & emergencies, lipids, syncope)
stem: What is the evidence-based approach to laboratory testing in preoperative cardiovascular evaluation?
answer: Tests are ordered based on identified conditions and expected surgical procedure; no routine panel is supported; the history and focused physical examination drive selective testing.
rationale: Routine preoperative testing has not been shown to improve outcomes and generates false-positive results leading to unnecessary delays and further testing; targeted testing based on clinical indication is cost-effective and evidence-based.

domain: Internal medicine: cardiology (ACS, stable & unstable angina, heart failure, brady/tachyarrhythmias, valvular disease, hypertension & emergencies, lipids, syncope)
stem: Patients noncompliant with PAP therapy for OSA have elevated serum bicarbonate. Why is this specifically relevant to cardiovascular risk assessment?
answer: Elevated HCO3 indicates chronic CO2 retention and OHS; these patients have pulmonary hypertension and right heart compromise that significantly elevates cardiovascular perioperative risk beyond what the OSA diagnosis alone suggests.
rationale: OHS with pulmonary hypertension adds right ventricular dysfunction to the cardiac risk profile; these patients may decompensate with fluid shifts, positive pressure ventilation changes, or postoperative hypoxemia.

domain: Internal medicine: cardiology (ACS, stable & unstable angina, heart failure, brady/tachyarrhythmias, valvular disease, hypertension & emergencies, lipids, syncope)
stem: The perioperative specialist's evaluation integrates what foundational elements alongside the standard history and physical?
answer: The perioperative specialist enhances standard H&P with assessment of functional capacity (METs), risk calculators (RCRI, MICA), medication reconciliation, and procedure-specific risk.
rationale: Functional capacity below 4 METs (unable to climb a flight of stairs) combined with elevated surgical risk identifies patients who may benefit from further cardiac testing; integrating these elements personalizes risk stratification.

domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: Fat embolism syndrome is diagnosed by what characteristic physical finding, and what other diagnostic methods may demonstrate fat emboli?
answer: Petechiae on the chest, upper extremities, axillae, and conjunctiva are characteristic; fat globules may occasionally be seen in the retina by ophthalmoscopy, in urine, or in sputum.
rationale: Fat emboli from long bone or pelvic fractures enter the venous system and traverse the pulmonary circulation; they cause a characteristic triad of hypoxemia, neurological dysfunction, and petechiae 24-72 hours post-injury.

topic: Pulmonary Embolism: Risk Factors and Classification
domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: Capnography shows decreased EtCO2 in pulmonary embolism. What is the specific mechanism?
answer: PE creates dead space (ventilated but unperfused alveoli); mixed expired CO2 is diluted by dead-space gas, reducing EtCO2; simultaneously arterial PaCO2 rises because CO2 cannot be exhaled efficiently, widening the EtCO2-PaCO2 gradient.
rationale: EtCO2 reflects CO2 from perfused alveoli only; in PE, perfusion is redirected, increasing physiologic dead space and diluting exhaled CO2, providing a real-time hemodynamic monitoring signal.
confusable_with: Bronchospasm (EtCO2 rises with prolonged upsloping trace)

topic: Pulmonary Embolism: Risk Factors and Classification
domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: In direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) therapy for atrial fibrillation with moderate-severe mitral stenosis, which anticoagulant remains indicated and why?
answer: Vitamin K antagonists (warfarin) remain indicated for moderate-severe rheumatic mitral stenosis or mechanical heart valves; DOACs are not approved in these settings based on clinical trial data showing inferior stroke prevention.
rationale: DOACs were not studied in rheumatic mitral stenosis (high thrombus burden, high valve gradient) or mechanical valves (dabigatran failed in mechanical valve trial); VKA with INR 2-3 remains standard of care.

source.book: Society Guideline: Guideline   ACC AHA 2023 Atrial Fibrillation

topic: Pulmonary Embolism: Risk Factors and Classification
domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: Pulmonary embolism causes shunt physiology in what way?
answer: PE primarily causes dead space (perfusion loss to ventilated lung); however, atelectasis distal to obstruction and reflex bronchoconstriction create areas of low V/Q ratio contributing to hypoxemia; severe PE may open a PFO causing right-to-left shunting.
rationale: The hypoxemia of PE is multifactorial: dead space raises CO2 but other mechanisms (low V/Q, PFO shunt, reduced mixed venous O2) cause the arterial hypoxemia that does not fully correct with 100% O2 in severe PE.
confusable_with: Pure shunt physiology (no response to O2 increase)

topic: Pulmonary Embolism: Risk Factors and Classification
domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: In the context of VTE in cancer patients, what classification aspect is most clinically relevant when selecting prophylaxis agents?
answer: Renal function: LMWH is preferred over UFH in cancer patients with adequate renal function; UFH is preferred when GFR is significantly reduced; DOACs (rivaroxaban, edoxaban) have shown benefit in selected cancer-VTE.
rationale: Cancer-associated VTE has higher recurrence and bleeding rates than non-cancer VTE; agent selection must balance efficacy (LMWH superior to warfarin in cancer-VTE) against renal clearance and bleeding risk from tumor-related sites.

topic: Pulmonary Embolism: Risk Factors and Classification
domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: In massive PE causing cardiac arrest or hemodynamic collapse, what is the key perioperative anesthetic consideration?
answer: Potential anesthetic interactions with hemodynamic instability are serious enough to potentially delay elective surgery; in emergency PE with cardiovascular collapse, vasopressors and thrombolysis take precedence over anesthetic management.
rationale: PE-induced right ventricular failure makes patients exquisitely sensitive to vasodilatory anesthetic agents; induction of anesthesia in massive PE can precipitate cardiac arrest; understanding this shapes emergency decision-making.

topic: Pulmonary Embolism: Risk Factors and Classification
domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: Which ECG finding pattern is classically associated with pulmonary embolism?
answer: ECG may show ischemic ST-segment changes and the S1Q3T3 pattern (S wave in lead I, Q wave and T-wave inversion in lead III), right heart strain, right bundle branch block, and sinus tachycardia—the most common finding.
rationale: Acute RV pressure overload from PE distorts ventricular geometry; S1Q3T3 reflects right axis deviation and right heart strain; sinus tachycardia is present in most cases but is nonspecific.
confusable_with: Inferior MI (Q waves in III but also in II and aVF)

domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: In neonates with meconium aspiration, what happens when the neonate initiates respiration at birth?
answer: Meconium moves from the trachea and large airways down toward the periphery, causing ball-valve obstruction with air trapping, hyperinflation, and potentially pneumothorax; chemical pneumonitis from meconium also occurs.
rationale: Thick meconium is a physical and chemical obstruction; its peripheral migration causes uneven air trapping, leading to overdistension and rupture of alveoli (pneumothorax) while simultaneously causing inflammation.

domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: Prematurity is defined as birth before what gestational age, and how does this differ from small for gestational age?
answer: Prematurity: birth before 37 weeks gestation; small for gestational age (SGA): age-adjusted weight below the 5th percentile (can be full-term or premature); these are distinct concepts with different pathophysiologies.
rationale: Premature infants have immature organ systems (surfactant deficiency, incomplete alveolar development); SGA infants have intrauterine growth restriction (placental insufficiency) and may have different respiratory complications.

domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: During post-cardiac arrest care, when should targeted temperature management (TTM) be initiated relative to percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI)?
answer: PCI should not be delayed to institute TTM; both are administered concurrently when possible.
rationale: Concurrent PCI and TTM address the two main causes of post-cardiac arrest mortality (obstructive coronary disease and reperfusion brain injury) simultaneously; delaying either worsens neurological and cardiac outcomes.

domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: Chronic respiratory acidosis has a different compensatory pattern than acute respiratory acidosis. What is the key difference?
answer: In chronic respiratory acidosis, renal compensation raises plasma HCO3 approximately 4 mEq/L for each 10 mmHg rise in PaCO2 after 3-5 days; acute respiratory acidosis has only 1 mEq/L HCO3 rise per 10 mmHg PaCO2 (buffering alone).
rationale: The acute 1:10 ratio reflects hemoglobin and protein buffering; the chronic 4:10 ratio reflects maximal renal H+ excretion and HCO3 regeneration, allowing near-normal pH despite persistent hypercapnia.
confusable_with: Metabolic alkalosis (elevated HCO3 with low PaCO2 not high)

domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: Beta-agonists promote cellular K+ uptake in acute hyperkalemia associated with massive transfusion. What other hemodynamic benefit does low-dose epinephrine infusion provide simultaneously?
answer: Low-dose epinephrine infusion rapidly decreases plasma K+ (through beta-2-mediated cellular uptake) and provides inotropic support, addressing both the hyperkalemia and the myocardial depression of massive transfusion simultaneously.
rationale: Massive transfusion delivers large K+ loads (from stored pRBCs) and citrate (causing hypocalcemia and cardiac depression); epinephrine addresses both hyperkalemia (cellular uptake) and myocardial depression (positive inotropy).

domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: HFNC in hypoxemic respiratory failure reduced mortality in one major trial compared to standard oxygen or NIV. What limitation should be noted?
answer: HFNC reduced mortality without reducing intubation rates; if HFNC fails and intubation is delayed due to apparent comfort, outcome may worsen (the 'ROX index' helps identify early failure); the mortality benefit may relate to comfort, diaphragm function, or patient selection.
rationale: HFNC provides high-flow humidified oxygen, reduces nasopharyngeal dead space, and offers mild CPAP; early failure identification is critical to avoid delaying intubation in deteriorating patients.

domain: Internal medicine: pulmonology (COPD, asthma, pulmonary embolism, pneumonia, ILD, pleural effusion, pneumothorax, hypoxemic & hypercapnic respiratory failure, OSA)
stem: Renal replacement therapy may be required in acute kidney injury, and what mode is preferred in hemodynamically unstable patients?
answer: Continuous renal replacement therapy (CRRT) is preferred over intermittent hemodialysis in hemodynamically unstable patients because it provides slower, gentler fluid and solute removal without causing the rapid osmolar shifts and hypotension of IHD.
rationale: IHD causes rapid fluid shifts that reduce preload and drop blood pressure in unstable patients; CRRT's continuous low-rate clearance maintains hemodynamic stability while achieving equivalent solute and fluid removal over 24 hours.

domain: Internal medicine: endocrinology (diabetes & inpatient glucose, DKA & HHS, thyroid disorders & storm, adrenal insufficiency, calcium disorders, pituitary)
stem: SIADH is characterized by what combination of serum and urine findings?
answer: Serum hyponatremia and hypoosmolarity; urine hypernatremia (urine Na >30 mEq/L) and hyperosmolarity (concentrated urine); patient is euvolemic or mildly hypervolemic.
rationale: Excess ADH causes free water retention, diluting serum sodium; the kidney continues to excrete sodium at a normal or elevated rate despite hyponatremia (inappropriate natriuresis), producing the characteristic high urine Na.
confusable_with: Cerebral salt wasting (hypovolemic, also high urine Na)

domain: Internal medicine: endocrinology (diabetes & inpatient glucose, DKA & HHS, thyroid disorders & storm, adrenal insufficiency, calcium disorders, pituitary)
stem: The maximum safe rate of sodium correction in SIADH is what, and what complication results from over-rapid correction?
answer: Maximum correction rate is less than 8-10 mEq/L in 24 hours; over-rapid correction causes osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis), an irreversible neurologic injury.
rationale: Chronic hyponatremia allows brain adaptation by reducing intracellular osmoles; rapid sodium correction creates a hyperosmolar gradient that draws water out of brain cells, demyelinating myelin sheaths in the pons.

domain: Internal medicine: endocrinology (diabetes & inpatient glucose, DKA & HHS, thyroid disorders & storm, adrenal insufficiency, calcium disorders, pituitary)
stem: The key differentiating feature between SIADH and cerebral salt wasting (CSW) is what?
answer: Volume status: SIADH patients are euvolemic or mildly hypervolemic; CSW patients are hypovolemic; both conditions have low serum sodium and high urine sodium, making volume assessment critical.
rationale: CSW occurs from inappropriate natriuresis that depletes total body sodium and volume; SIADH involves water retention without sodium depletion; treatment differs fundamentally (fluid restriction for SIADH vs. saline replacement for CSW).

source.book: StatPearls: StatPearls   SIADH (Syndrome of Inappropriate ADH)

domain: Internal medicine: endocrinology (diabetes & inpatient glucose, DKA & HHS, thyroid disorders & storm, adrenal insufficiency, calcium disorders, pituitary)
stem: When should 3% hypertonic saline be used cautiously in SIADH-related hyponatremia?
answer: 3% hypertonic saline should be used cautiously when the patient has severe neurological symptoms (confusion, seizures, coma) from hyponatremia; correction must still be limited to less than 8-10 mEq/L per 24 hours.
rationale: Severe symptomatic hyponatremia (seizures) requires faster correction to prevent cerebral herniation, but the rate must be carefully controlled to avoid osmotic demyelination; 3% saline is titrated to symptom resolution, then slowed.

domain: Internal medicine: endocrinology (diabetes & inpatient glucose, DKA & HHS, thyroid disorders & storm, adrenal insufficiency, calcium disorders, pituitary)
stem: Nonosmotic ADH secretion is activated by volume depletion. At what level of intravascular volume deficit does this occur?
answer: Nonosmotic ADH secretion is activated when intravascular volume deficit approaches 5-10%; at this point the volume-sensing mechanism overrides osmotic regulation to preserve cardiac output.
rationale: ADH secretion is normally regulated by plasma osmolality; severe volume depletion activates baroreceptors that override osmotic suppression, causing ADH-mediated free water retention even in hyponatremia.

domain: Internal medicine: endocrinology (diabetes & inpatient glucose, DKA & HHS, thyroid disorders & storm, adrenal insufficiency, calcium disorders, pituitary)
stem: What other conditions must be excluded before diagnosing SIADH?
answer: Polydipsia, renal disease, diuretic use, heart failure, hypothyroidism, malignancies, hormone deficiency (adrenal insufficiency), and pseudohyponatremia must all be excluded.
rationale: SIADH is a diagnosis of exclusion; each alternative cause of hyponatremia has different pathophysiology and treatment; treating SIADH with fluid restriction when the cause is adrenal insufficiency (requiring steroids) would be harmful.

domain: Internal medicine: endocrinology (diabetes & inpatient glucose, DKA & HHS, thyroid disorders & storm, adrenal insufficiency, calcium disorders, pituitary)
stem: Congestive heart failure and nephrotic syndrome both cause hyponatremia with different total body sodium status than SIADH. Why?
answer: CHF and nephrotic syndrome cause hyponatremia with HIGH total body sodium and water (edematous states) because effective arterial volume depletion triggers nonosmotic ADH; SIADH has normal-to-slightly elevated total body sodium with excess free water only.
rationale: In CHF/nephrotic syndrome, reduced effective circulatory volume stimulates ADH and RAAS, retaining both sodium and water; but water retention exceeds sodium retention, causing hyponatremia despite total body sodium excess.

enabling_conditions: CNS disease (meningitis, SAH, head injury), pulmonary disease (pneumonia, TB, positive pressure ventilation), malignancy (small cell lung, CNS tumors), drugs (SSRIs, carbamazepine, cyclophosphamide, NSAIDs)
pathophysiology: Excess ADH causes collecting duct aquaporin-2 insertion, renal free water retention, volume expansion, and dilutional hyponatremia; natriuresis continues despite low serum Na (inappropriate)
time_course: Chronic (>48h) hyponatremia is asymptomatic until severe; acute hyponatremia (brain adaptation incomplete) causes early cerebral edema
key_features: Euvolemia or mild hypervolemia; serum Na <135; serum osmolality <275; urine osmolality >100; urine Na >30 mEq/L; no edema, no volume depletion
consequence_if_missed: Seizures, brain herniation from cerebral edema; osmotic demyelination from over-rapid correction

domain: Anesthetic pharmacology (inhaled agents, IV induction agents, opioids, neuromuscular blockers & reversal, local anesthetics, benzodiazepines, vasoactive/adjunct drugs)
stem: Dexmedetomidine is an alpha-2 agonist. What is the mechanism and site of its sedative versus analgesic/sympatholytic effects?
answer: Sedation: locus coeruleus alpha-2A receptor activation produces NREM-like sleep; sympatholysis: presynaptic alpha-2 receptor activation in the spinal cord and periphery reduces norepinephrine release, decreasing HR, BP, and pain transmission.
rationale: Alpha-2A receptors in the locus coeruleus mediate hypnosis; spinal alpha-2A/C receptors inhibit nociceptive transmission; peripheral presynaptic alpha-2 receptors reduce sympathetic outflow—each mechanism is anatomically distinct.

domain: Anesthetic pharmacology (inhaled agents, IV induction agents, opioids, neuromuscular blockers & reversal, local anesthetics, benzodiazepines, vasoactive/adjunct drugs)
stem: Phenylephrine is a pure alpha-1 agonist given for spinal hypotension. What is the dose range for IV bolus in adults, and what is its duration of action?
answer: Phenylephrine 50-100 mcg IV bolus (0.5-1 mcg/kg) for spinal-induced hypotension in adults; duration of action is short.
rationale: Phenylephrine's selective alpha-1 agonism causes pure vasoconstriction without cardiac stimulation; in obstetric spinal anesthesia it is preferred over ephedrine for maintaining uteroplacental flow without maternal tachycardia.
confusable_with: Ephedrine (alpha + beta, preferred for bradycardia + hypotension)

domain: Anesthetic pharmacology (inhaled agents, IV induction agents, opioids, neuromuscular blockers & reversal, local anesthetics, benzodiazepines, vasoactive/adjunct drugs)
stem: Target-controlled infusion (TCI) employs what technology, and what pharmacokinetic model drives it?
answer: TCI uses computerized infusion pump software with pharmacokinetic models (Marsh or Schnider for propofol; Minto for remifentanil) to deliver drug targeting a specified plasma or effect-site concentration.
rationale: TCI integrates drug distribution and elimination kinetics to continuously adjust infusion rate, maintaining stable predicted drug concentrations without manual titration—more precise than manual infusion for agent pharmacokinetics.

domain: Anesthetic pharmacology (inhaled agents, IV induction agents, opioids, neuromuscular blockers & reversal, local anesthetics, benzodiazepines, vasoactive/adjunct drugs)
stem: The combination of opioids and benzodiazepines markedly reduces arterial blood pressure. What is the mechanism?
answer: Combined opioid-benzodiazepine administration markedly reduces arterial blood pressure and peripheral vascular resistance through synergistic CNS and cardiovascular depression.
rationale: Opioids depress sympathetic tone; benzodiazepines potentiate GABA-mediated CNS depression including vasomotor centers; together they produce greater hemodynamic depression than either alone.

domain: Anesthetic pharmacology (inhaled agents, IV induction agents, opioids, neuromuscular blockers & reversal, local anesthetics, benzodiazepines, vasoactive/adjunct drugs)
stem: Benzodiazepines reduce minimum alveolar concentration (MAC) of volatile anesthetics by approximately how much?
answer: Benzodiazepines reduce MAC of volatile anesthetics by as much as 30%.
rationale: Benzodiazepines' GABA-A potentiation produces sedation that reduces the CNS stimulation required by volatile agents to maintain anesthesia, thereby reducing the MAC needed for immobility.
confusable_with: Opioids (reduce MAC dose-dependently but cannot eliminate it)

domain: Anesthetic pharmacology (inhaled agents, IV induction agents, opioids, neuromuscular blockers & reversal, local anesthetics, benzodiazepines, vasoactive/adjunct drugs)
stem: The principal pharmacodynamic change associated with aging that affects anesthetic management is what?
answer: Reduced anesthetic requirement: MAC decreases with age; older patients require less volatile anesthetic and lower doses of IV agents for equivalent effect.
rationale: Age-related reduction in brain cell mass, reduced neural connectivity, and altered neurotransmitter function all contribute to increased anesthetic sensitivity; failure to reduce doses in elderly patients causes hemodynamic instability and delayed emergence.

domain: Anesthetic pharmacology (inhaled agents, IV induction agents, opioids, neuromuscular blockers & reversal, local anesthetics, benzodiazepines, vasoactive/adjunct drugs)
stem: What is MAC-amnesia, and how does it compare numerically to MAC (MAC-awake vs MAC-immobility)?
answer: MAC-amnesia is the concentration preventing recall in 50% of a population; it is less well-defined but is lower than MAC-awake; MAC-awake is approximately 0.55-0.64 MAC (immobility); MAC-immobility (standard MAC) is the benchmark.
rationale: The hierarchy MAC-amnesia < MAC-awake < MAC-immobility reflects increasing CNS suppression requirements; ensuring MAC-amnesia is exceeded is critical for preventing awareness under anesthesia.

topic: Diagnostic Test Performance and Clinical Decision-Making
domain: Anesthesia: basic & clinical sciences (relevant anatomy, respiratory/cardiac/renal/neuro physiology, pharmacokinetics/dynamics principles, physics of gases & flow, statistics)
stem: AKI is defined by what two criteria according to KDIGO 2012 guidelines?
answer: AKI is defined by an abrupt decrease in kidney function: serum creatinine rise of 0.3 mg/dL or more within 48 hours, OR rise to 1.5x or more from baseline within 7 days, OR urine output less than 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 or more hours.
rationale: The dual criteria (creatinine-based and urine output-based) capture different aspects of AKI: small acute creatinine rises predict worse outcomes even before reaching traditional thresholds; oliguria is an early functional sign.

topic: Diagnostic Test Performance and Clinical Decision-Making
domain: Anesthesia: basic & clinical sciences (relevant anatomy, respiratory/cardiac/renal/neuro physiology, pharmacokinetics/dynamics principles, physics of gases & flow, statistics)
stem: Serum creatinine approximates GFR only at steady state. What is the clinical implication when creatinine is rising rapidly?
answer: When creatinine rises more than 1 mg/dL per day, GFR must be assumed to be less than 10 mL/min regardless of the absolute creatinine value; GFR cannot be estimated during non-steady-state AKI.
rationale: The creatinine-GFR relationship assumes equilibrium between creatinine production and clearance; in acute injury, creatinine is accumulating and the standard equations (CKD-EPI, MDRD) overestimate GFR.
confusable_with: Stable CKD (creatinine accurately reflects GFR at steady state)

topic: Diagnostic Test Performance and Clinical Decision-Making
domain: Anesthesia: basic & clinical sciences (relevant anatomy, respiratory/cardiac/renal/neuro physiology, pharmacokinetics/dynamics principles, physics of gases & flow, statistics)
stem: What systematic approach should be used to evaluate a patient with suspected AKI?
answer: Differentiate prerenal (FENa <1%, BUN/Cr >20, concentrated urine), intrinsic renal (FENa >2%, granular casts, isosthenuria), and postrenal (hydronephrosis on ultrasound) causes using clinical assessment, lab values, and imaging.
rationale: Each AKI category has distinct mechanisms and treatments: prerenal requires fluids or improved cardiac output; intrinsic renal requires supportive care; postrenal requires obstruction relief—misdiagnosis leads to harmful management.

topic: Diagnostic Test Performance and Clinical Decision-Making
domain: Anesthesia: basic & clinical sciences (relevant anatomy, respiratory/cardiac/renal/neuro physiology, pharmacokinetics/dynamics principles, physics of gases & flow, statistics)
stem: AKD (Acute Kidney Disease) differs from AKI in what temporal definition?
answer: AKD defines kidney dysfunction between 7 days (where AKI ends) and 90 days after an acute insult; it bridges AKI and CKD, identifying a recovery or progression window.
rationale: AKD recognizes that kidney injury trajectories fall on a continuum; patients in the AKD window have opportunity for recovery interventions (nephrotoxin avoidance, blood pressure optimization) before permanent CKD is established.

topic: Diagnostic Test Performance and Clinical Decision-Making
domain: Anesthesia: basic & clinical sciences (relevant anatomy, respiratory/cardiac/renal/neuro physiology, pharmacokinetics/dynamics principles, physics of gases & flow, statistics)
stem: ACE inhibitors and ARBs are common AKI precipitants. By what mechanism do they cause AKI, and in what clinical situations is this most likely?
answer: ACE inhibitors/ARBs block angiotensin II-mediated efferent arteriolar constriction; in states of reduced renal perfusion (renal artery stenosis, heart failure, volume depletion), they drop GFR by eliminating the compensatory efferent vasoconstriction.
rationale: Normal glomerular filtration pressure requires a balance of afferent and efferent arteriolar tone; in reduced perfusion states, angiotensin II selectively constricts the efferent arteriole to maintain GFR; blocking this with ACE-I/ARB precipitates AKI.
confusable_with: NSAIDs (reduce afferent dilation, also precipitate AKI)

topic: Diagnostic Test Performance and Clinical Decision-Making
domain: Anesthesia: basic & clinical sciences (relevant anatomy, respiratory/cardiac/renal/neuro physiology, pharmacokinetics/dynamics principles, physics of gases & flow, statistics)
stem: In GFR measurement for cancer patients receiving carboplatin, cisplatin, or methotrexate, why is measured GFR (mGFR) preferred over estimated GFR?
answer: mGFR (by inulin or iohexol clearance) is preferred for precise dosing of nephrotoxic chemotherapy because eGFR equations have meaningful inaccuracy in cancer patients (muscle wasting, altered creatinine production) that can cause under- or overdosing.
rationale: Carboplatin dosing uses the Calvert formula incorporating GFR; using an inaccurate eGFR causes under-exposure (treatment failure) or overdose (severe myelosuppression); mGFR reduces this risk in the highest-stakes dosing situations.

topic: Diagnostic Test Performance and Clinical Decision-Making
domain: Anesthesia: basic & clinical sciences (relevant anatomy, respiratory/cardiac/renal/neuro physiology, pharmacokinetics/dynamics principles, physics of gases & flow, statistics)
stem: Drugs can impair creatinine excretion without changing GFR. What clinical clue helps distinguish drug-induced creatinine rise from true AKI?
answer: If creatinine rises with an appropriate drug (e.g., trimethoprim, cimetidine block tubular creatinine secretion) but BUN remains stable and urine output is maintained, this suggests drug-induced creatinine elevation without true GFR reduction.
rationale: Tubular creatinine secretion contributes to total creatinine clearance; drugs blocking secretion raise serum creatinine without reducing GFR; stable BUN and preserved urine output despite rising creatinine distinguishes this from true AKI.

domain: Anesthetic pharmacology (inhaled agents, IV induction agents, opioids, neuromuscular blockers & reversal, local anesthetics, benzodiazepines, vasoactive/adjunct drugs)
stem: The basic pharmacokinetic principles of clinical pharmacology include what key concepts for describing anesthetic drug behavior?
answer: Pharmacokinetics describes drug absorption, distribution, metabolism, and elimination; key parameters include volume of distribution, clearance, half-life, and bioavailability; these determine the time course of drug effect.
rationale: Understanding PK allows prediction of drug onset, duration, and accumulation; anesthetic drug selection and dosing are fundamentally PK-driven to ensure adequate effect during surgery and recovery after procedure.

domain: Anesthetic pharmacology (inhaled agents, IV induction agents, opioids, neuromuscular blockers & reversal, local anesthetics, benzodiazepines, vasoactive/adjunct drugs)
stem: CYP3A4-inducing antiepileptic drugs significantly affect DOAC levels. What is the clinical implication for patients on antiepileptic therapy who also take rivaroxaban or apixaban?
answer: CYP-inducing antiepileptic drugs (e.g., carbamazepine, phenytoin) significantly lower DOAC (rivaroxaban, apixaban) plasma levels, potentially rendering anticoagulation subtherapeutic and increasing stroke/VTE risk.
rationale: CYP3A4 inducers upregulate hepatic and intestinal metabolism of factor Xa inhibitors, reducing drug exposure (AUC) by 50-75%; this drug interaction can cause anticoagulation failure and requires either dose adjustment or switch to a non-CYP3A4-cleared anticoagulant.

source.book: Society Guideline: Guideline   ACC AHA 2023 Atrial Fibrillation

domain: Anesthetic pharmacology (inhaled agents, IV induction agents, opioids, neuromuscular blockers & reversal, local anesthetics, benzodiazepines, vasoactive/adjunct drugs)
stem: Potency describes the amount of drug required to elicit an effect (C50). How does potency differ from efficacy?
answer: Potency refers to the concentration producing 50% of maximum effect (C50/ED50); efficacy refers to the maximum effect a drug can produce regardless of dose. A drug can be highly potent (low C50) but have low efficacy (limited maximum effect).
rationale: Two drugs targeting the same receptor may require different doses (potency) and may produce different maximum effects (efficacy); partial agonists have limited efficacy at full receptor occupancy while full agonists can produce maximal response.

domain: Anesthetic pharmacology (inhaled agents, IV induction agents, opioids, neuromuscular blockers & reversal, local anesthetics, benzodiazepines, vasoactive/adjunct drugs)
stem: Cimetidine reduces hepatic drug metabolism. By what mechanism, and what class of drugs is most affected?
answer: Cimetidine inhibits hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes (CYP1A2, CYP2C9, CYP3A4) and reduces liver blood flow; drugs with high hepatic extraction ratios (e.g., propranolol, lidocaine) are most affected.
rationale: High-extraction drugs have clearance determined primarily by liver blood flow; drugs with low extraction are more affected by enzyme inhibition; cimetidine's dual mechanism (enzyme inhibition + reduced blood flow) makes it a potent inhibitor of hepatic drug metabolism.

domain: Anesthetic pharmacology (inhaled agents, IV induction agents, opioids, neuromuscular blockers & reversal, local anesthetics, benzodiazepines, vasoactive/adjunct drugs)
stem: Physiologic versus chronologic age assessment is important when dosing anesthetic drugs in older patients. Why?
answer: Physiologic age (functional reserve, comorbidities, body habitus, exercise tolerance) better predicts anesthetic drug requirements than chronologic age; a healthy 75-year-old may need similar doses to a younger patient, while a frail 65-year-old may need substantially less.
rationale: Pharmacokinetic differences in aging (reduced Vd for hydrophilic drugs, reduced hepatic clearance, reduced renal clearance) are variable; physiologic age captures these functional differences more accurately than birth year.

domain: Anesthetic pharmacology (inhaled agents, IV induction agents, opioids, neuromuscular blockers & reversal, local anesthetics, benzodiazepines, vasoactive/adjunct drugs)
stem: Opioid-induced hyperalgesia (OIH) is a recognized phenomenon. What is the clinical controversy regarding its perioperative significance?
answer: Whether acute tolerance and OIH play important roles in perioperative management is controversial; animal and human study data are inconsistent; high-dose intraoperative remifentanil is most strongly associated with possible OIH.
rationale: OIH may explain increased postoperative pain and opioid requirements in some patients receiving high intraoperative opioid doses; the clinical magnitude is debated, but it supports multimodal analgesia to minimize opioid doses.

domain: Anesthetic pharmacology (inhaled agents, IV induction agents, opioids, neuromuscular blockers & reversal, local anesthetics, benzodiazepines, vasoactive/adjunct drugs)
stem: Dose adjustment of anticancer drugs including carboplatin and cisplatin should incorporate measured GFR rather than estimated GFR. What is the additional consideration for nephrotoxic drugs in patients with CKD?
answer: Nephrotoxic drugs should have doses adjusted based on actual kidney function; in CKD patients receiving carboplatin/cisplatin, mGFR is preferred to avoid underdosing (treatment failure) or overdosing (severe nephrotoxicity and myelosuppression).
rationale: These drugs are cleared renally and are themselves nephrotoxic; dosing using inaccurate eGFR in CKD creates a bidirectional risk—underdose fails the cancer patient, overdose accelerates kidney failure and bone marrow toxicity.
